title: DC Motor: The Workhorse
description: Component lesson. The exact motor that turns ARIA's wheels — and what happens inside when you ask it for more than it can give.

content.value: The previous lesson's trick — current through a coil near a magnet, mounted to spin — needs one more piece to actually keep turning: something to flip the current's direction at exactly the right moment every half-turn, or the coil would just swing to a stop lined up with the magnet, like a compass needle settling.

That job belongs to the commutator, a split metal ring that rotates with the coil, and the brushes, two spring-loaded contacts that stay still and press against it. As the commutator spins past the brushes, the split flips which way current flows through the coil at exactly the half-turn point — so the push never has a chance to run out.

brushes (fixed) --press against--> commutator (spins with coil)

half-turn 1: current flows one way   -> coil pushed forward
split passes under the brushes       -> current direction flips
half-turn 2: current flows other way -> coil still pushed forward

content.title: ⚙️ Voltage and load
content.hint: Crank the load up while voltage is low. Watch what happens to the current when the motor can't turn anymore.

content.value: More voltage means more push, so RPM climbs. But push a real motor with a stronger load than its current voltage can overcome, and something specific happens: the rotor can't turn, yet the coil is still trying to draw current — with nothing spinning to generate the usual back-resistance, current spikes upward instead of doing useful work. That's a stall, and it's exactly how motors overheat and burn out for real.

Part          Small brushed DC gear motor (TT motor)
Voltage       3–6V typical hobby range
No-load RPM   ~200 RPM (after gearing)
Stall current  several times higher than running current
Price         ≈ ₹60–100

That gearbox matters: a bare motor spins fast but has very little turning force. Gearing trades some of that speed for a lot more torque — enough to actually move a chassis. You'll meet gear ratios properly in Module 6.

Key takeaway: brushes and a commutator keep a DC motor's push going continuously by flipping current direction each half-turn. Overload a motor beyond what its voltage can supply and it stalls — current spikes instead of turning into motion.

quiz.question: What is the commutator's job inside a DC motor?
options: To flip the current's direction through the coil at each half-turn, so the push never runs out
To supply power from the battery
quiz.explain: Without that flip, the coil would just swing to a stop aligned with the fixed magnet, like a compass needle.

quiz.question: In the widget, what happens to current when you push the load past what the voltage can overcome?
options: It spikes upward, while RPM drops to zero — a stall
quiz.explain: A stalled motor still tries to draw current, but with nothing spinning to help regulate it, current climbs instead of producing motion.

quiz.question: Why does a stalled motor risk burning out?
options: The spiking current turns into heat inside the motor with nowhere useful to go
Stalling makes the motor spin faster
Stalled motors are always disconnected automatically
quiz.explain: All that extra current has to go somewhere — with the motor not converting it into motion, it becomes heat, which is exactly what damages windings over time.
